contributions: A measured characterisation of mixed RL rollout serving showing verifiable-reward, human-feedback and agentic rollouts differ by orders of magnitude in input and output length, KV residency and dominant cost, plus a tool-gap measurement (6.6 against 22.7 percent across two models) showing model inference time understates cache residency.
A demonstrated prefill-eviction feedback loop under which placement-only routing collapses to a 4.5 percent prefix-cache hit rate at a ceiling admission-controlled policies tolerate.
Per-class protected KV quotas derived from footprint and residency, which bound what a class may commit without prescribing trainer sampling.
An ordered ablation separating class-agnostic admission, per-class allocation and residency-time weighting, each contributing separately on both models.
Mixture-fidelity reporting alongside throughput: total-variation distance from the trainer target falls from 4.14 to 2.71 percentage points while rollout throughput rises 35.6 percent.
limitations: The authors state that MISA-T assumes requests carry workload labels and depends on timely serving-state reports, and that delayed or incomplete snapshots degrade the KV-demand estimates and caps. Reader-visible additions: everything rests on one production trace from one deployment, and the paper says explicitly that the class profiles in Table 1 characterise that deployment rather than defining the workload types -- so the residency-time term's value is contingent on an agentic mixture with long retained prefixes. The end-to-end comparison is a single 50-iteration matched run on one model with no repeats. The task-score claim is a null result at that horizon (under 0.5 points on three SWE benchmarks) rather than evidence that fifty iterations of faster rollout produce a better policy, and the mixture deviation of 2.71 against 4.14 points is a single measurement without a spread. The baseline is a sweep-tuned router at its own best operating point for the rollout-only ablation, which is fair, but the headline collapse figure comes from running that baseline at a ceiling chosen for the admission policies.
method: Three controls at the routing layer, on top of rather than in place of cache-aware placement. Adaptive session admission regulates how many new sessions may enter from delayed and asynchronous serving-state reports, so the operating point does not have to be re-swept when the model, sequence lengths or mixture change; a base cap follows a moving session-length reference, and when confirmed prefix-hit degradation says the reference is lagging, the current cap is temporarily lowered. Workload-aware capacity allocation gives each class a block quota rather than sharing one class-agnostic pool, since a backlog of N unfinished sessions with mean footprint k and mean residency T represents roughly N*k*T block-time work; dividing a class's quota by its footprint yields an enforceable session cap that bounds how much protected KV that class can commit without prescribing how often the trainer samples it. Residency-time-aware accounting is the third term, added because model inference time alone understates how long an agentic session holds cache -- the tool gap outside model inference is 6.6 percent of agent task time on one model and 22.7 percent on the other.
one_liner: A routing-layer admission policy for RL post-training that treats admitting a rollout session as a commitment of KV-cache capacity, allocates protected capacity per workload class by footprint and observed residency time, and leaves the workload mixture itself under the trainer's control.
problem: Post-training pipelines now mix verifiable-reward, human-feedback and agentic rollouts on one asynchronous inference service, and the three have opposite serving profiles: verifiable-reward samples are short-input, decode-dominated; agentic sessions carry long accumulated prefixes retained across tool-interleaved turns; human-feedback sits between. Prefix-aware routing decides where a request goes but not how many sessions may compete for cache, and under a permissive concurrency ceiling that omission produces a positive feedback loop -- admitting new sessions expands the resident working set, evicts reusable continuations, turns later turns into cold prefill, lengthens queues, and creates more eviction pressure.

relevance.reasoning-training: An infrastructure paper, and the reason it belongs in the archive is that it measures what a mixed RL post-training run actually asks of a serving system -- agent rollouts with median 37,757-token inputs and 148-token outputs sharing a pool with verifiable-reward rollouts at 156 in and 47,583 out. Those are not variants of one workload, and the collapse result shows what happens when they are treated as one: prefix-cache hit rate falls from 92.4 percent to 4.5 through a self-reinforcing eviction loop, at a concurrency ceiling that an admission-controlled policy tolerates. The point that generalises beyond systems work is the mixture-fidelity constraint the paper insists on: a scheduler that speeds up rollouts by preferentially serving the cheap ones has silently changed the training distribution, so throughput must be reported alongside the consumed mixture. This paper reports both (total-variation distance 2.71 against the baseline's 4.14 points) and treats the target as the trainer's to set. Any archive entry about what a training signal costs should record that the cost is not uniform across the rollout kinds a mixed pipeline draws from, and that the scheduler sits between the trainer's intended distribution and the one the policy is actually trained on.

results: The workload trace is itself a contribution: under a 128K context limit, agent requests have median input 37,757 tokens and median output 148, while verifiable-reward requests have median input 156 and median output 47,583, with p95 at 130,815 -- three orders of magnitude apart in both directions. Rollout-only ablation against a sweep-tuned vLLM Router: MISA-T improves sample rate by 53.3 percent on Step3.7 and 43.6 percent on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, with prefix-cache hit rates of 97.8 and 95.3 percent. The ablation is ordered and each control is separately worth something: class-agnostic session admission gives +11.7 and +19.3, adding per-class allocation gives +23.3 and +30.9 (that is 10.4 and 9.7 percent over session admission), and adding residency-time weighting gives +53.3 and +43.6 (a further 24.3 and 9.7 percent). The failure mode is demonstrated rather than argued: raising the placement-only router to the same permissive concurrency ceiling the admission policies use collapses it -- request throughput down 52.5 percent, prefill 57.3, decode 38.5, and prefix-cache hit rate from 92.4 percent to 4.5. Every admission-based policy interrupts that loop. End to end over a matched 50-iteration Step3.7 run: iteration time down 22.8 percent, sample rate up 35.6, prefill throughput up 33.6, decode up 38.0, prefix hit rate 74.5 to 96.2 percent -- lower than the rollout-only figure because weight synchronisation resets the caches each iteration and subsequent requests cold-prefill until reusable state reaccumulates. The mixture-fidelity result is the one that matters for correctness rather than speed: against a trainer target of 48.6/33.1/18.2 percent agent/RLVR/RLHF, MISA-T consumes 45.9/33.3/20.8 for a total-variation distance of 2.71 points against the baseline's 48.3/29.4/22.4 and 4.14 points -- so the faster scheduler also distorts the intended mixture less. Task scores are within 0.5 percentage points of the baseline on pass@4 for SWE-Pro, SWE-Verified and SWE-MTLG. A separate run with 1.3 TB of CPU KV offload keeps GPU KV utilisation at or above 90 percent through steady state and improves mean per-replica requests per minute by 35.6 percent, with the routing policy unchanged.
